title: Emergency fund: your first investment
hook: Before SIPs, before stocks: money you can reach in a day.
slides: What it is
Cash set aside only for real emergencies: a job loss, a medical bill, an urgent repair. It is not for holidays or a new phone.
How much
A common rule of thumb is 6 months of essential expenses. If your income is irregular or you have dependants, aim higher.
Where to keep it
Somewhere safe and quick to reach, such as a savings account, a sweep-in fixed deposit or a liquid fund. Return matters less than access.
Why it comes first
Without it, one bad month forces you to break investments at the wrong time or borrow at high interest.
takeaway: An emergency fund lets your long-term investments stay invested.

title: Term insurance in plain words
hook: The cheapest way to protect the people who depend on your income.
slides: What it is
Pure life cover. If the insured person dies during the policy term, the family receives the sum assured. If not, nothing is paid back.
Why it is cheap
There is no investment part, so the premium buys only protection. That is why a large cover costs relatively little.
How much cover
A common starting point is 10 to 15 times your annual income, adjusted for loans and future goals such as children's education.
Who needs it
Anyone with people who depend on their income. If nobody depends on you financially, you may not need it yet.
takeaway: Insurance is for protection. Investment is for growth. Mixing the two usually weakens both.

title: Health insurance: don't rely only on your employer
hook: One hospital bill can undo years of saving.
slides: The gap
Employer cover usually ends when the job ends, and the amount is often too small for a serious illness in a private hospital.
A personal policy
Your own policy stays with you across jobs. Buying while young and healthy usually means lower premiums and fewer exclusions.
Read the limits
Check room rent limits, waiting periods for existing illnesses, co-payment and what is excluded, before you need to claim.
Top-up plans
A super top-up plan can raise your total cover at a lower cost than a bigger base policy.
takeaway: Health cover protects your savings as much as your health.

title: Good debt, bad debt
hook: Not all loans are equal. The interest rate and the purpose tell you which is which.
slides: Expensive debt
Credit card balances and many personal loans carry very high interest. Paying these off is a guaranteed saving.
Useful debt
A home loan or education loan can build an asset or earning power, usually at a lower rate. It still has to be affordable.
The EMI test
A widely used guide: keep total EMIs within about 40% of take-home pay, so one shock does not break the budget.
Order of attack
Clear the highest-interest loan first. Then move to the next. Avoid borrowing to invest.
takeaway: Pay off costly debt before chasing returns. Few investments beat a 36% credit card rate.

title: The 50-30-20 budget
hook: A simple starting split for your take-home pay.
slides: 50% needs
Rent or EMI, groceries, bills, school fees, insurance premiums. The things you cannot skip.
30% wants
Eating out, travel, gadgets, subscriptions. Enjoy them, inside a limit.
20% future
Savings, investments and extra loan repayments. Treat this like a bill you pay yourself first.
Adjust it
In an expensive city, needs may take more than half. The split matters less than having one and tracking it.
takeaway: A budget is not a restriction. It is a plan for where your money goes.

title: Pay yourself first
hook: Most people save what is left after spending. Reverse the order.
slides: The idea
Move your savings out on salary day, before any spending. What remains is yours to spend without guilt.
Automate it
A SIP or a standing instruction removes the monthly decision. Discipline becomes the default.
Start small
Even a small amount builds the habit. Raise it every time your income rises.
Why it works
Spending expands to fill whatever is in the account. Saving first shrinks what is available to spend.
takeaway: Save first, spend the rest. Not the other way round.

title: Inflation: the silent tax
hook: Why ₹1 lakh today will not buy the same things in 10 years.
slides: What it does
Prices rise over time, so the same money buys less. At 6% inflation, costs roughly double in about 12 years.
Real return
What matters is return after inflation. A 7% deposit with 6% inflation grows your buying power by only about 1% a year, before tax.
Long-term goals
Retirement and education costs must be planned at future prices, not today's.
The trade-off
Assets that can beat inflation over long periods, such as equity, also fluctuate more in the short term.
takeaway: Money that does not grow faster than prices is slowly shrinking.

title: Retirement: start early or pay more later
hook: The cost of waiting ten years is larger than it looks.
slides: Time does the work
Money invested in your 20s and 30s has decades to compound. Later money has far less time.
An illustration
₹10,000 a month for 30 years at an assumed 12% grows to about ₹3.5 crore. For 20 years it is about ₹1 crore. Illustration only, not a projection.
Know your number
Estimate your yearly expenses in retirement at future prices, and how many years they must last.
Keep it separate
Money for retirement should not be the fund you dip into for cars or holidays.
takeaway: The best time to start was ten years ago. The next best is this month.

title: Goal-based investing
hook: Give every rupee a job and a date.
slides: Name the goal
House down payment in 5 years. Child's college in 12. Retirement in 25. Each has an amount and a deadline.
Match the horizon
Short-term goals need stability. Long-term goals can carry more equity, because there is time to recover from falls.
Separate buckets
Keeping goals separate stops a short-term need from disturbing a long-term plan.
Review yearly
As a goal comes closer, the usual practice is to move gradually towards safer assets.
takeaway: A goal with a date tells you how much risk you can afford.

title: Asset allocation
hook: How you split your money matters more than which fund you pick.
slides: The main assets
Equity for long-term growth, debt for stability, gold as a diversifier, cash for emergencies.
Why mix them
They do not all rise and fall together. A mix makes the journey smoother than any single asset.
Your mix
It depends on your goals, time horizon and how you react to falls. There is no single right answer.
Rebalance
Once a year, bring the mix back to plan. This means trimming what has run up and adding to what has lagged.
takeaway: Decide your mix first. Then choose products to fill it.

title: Credit score basics
hook: Three digits that decide your loan rate.
slides: What it is
A score built from your repayment history. Lenders use it to judge how reliably you repay.
What helps
Paying every EMI and card bill on time, and keeping card usage well below the limit.
What hurts
Missed payments, many loan applications in a short time, and settling a loan for less than the dues.
Check it
You are entitled to a free credit report each year from every credit bureau. Check it for errors.
takeaway: A good score can mean a lower interest rate on your biggest loans.

title: Nominations and a will
hook: Ten minutes of paperwork that saves your family months of trouble.
slides: Nominations
Add a nominee to every bank account, demat account, mutual fund folio and insurance policy. Check that old ones are still correct.
A will
A nominee is often only a custodian. A will states who finally inherits. It need not be complicated.
One list
Keep a simple record of accounts, policies and loans, and tell a trusted family member where it is.
Review it
Update after marriage, a child, or a death in the family.
takeaway: Your family should not have to search for what you built for them.

title: Lifestyle inflation
hook: Why a higher salary often does not feel like more money.
slides: What happens
Each raise is matched by a bigger car, a bigger rent, a costlier phone. Savings stay where they were.
The fix
Decide in advance: half of every raise goes to investments before it reaches your spending account.
Step-up SIP
Raising your SIP by a fixed percentage every year keeps your investing in line with your income.
Enjoy it too
The aim is not to live poorly. It is to let your savings grow at least as fast as your spending.
takeaway: Raise your savings every time your income rises.

title: Tax saving is not investing
hook: Buying a product only to save tax in March is a common mistake.
slides: Goal first
Ask what the money is for and when you need it. Then see which suitable option also saves tax.
Lock-ins
Many tax-saving products lock your money for years. Know the period before you commit.
Plan in April
Spreading tax-saving investments through the year avoids a rushed decision in the last month.
Regimes differ
India has two income tax regimes with different deductions. Which is better depends on your income and deductions; check with a tax professional.
takeaway: A bad product does not become good because it saves tax.
